question: In Canada, how can I tell from a package whether the whole food was irradiated or it just contains an irradiated ingredient?
generated_answer:
In Canada, irradiated whole foods and ingredients of irradiated foods sold in stores must be labelled with a statement indicating that they were treated with ionizing radiation. You will find a statement similar to this on the package:

Irradiated, treat with food irradiation

or

treated with radiation

Whole foods that are not normally pre-packaged and foods that are not required to have a label (like fresh fruits and vegetables) are also required to be labelled, if they have been irradiated. This label must be displayed either at the point of sale (for example, on the bin where the item is sold) or on a nearby sign. What foods are most commonly irradiated and why? A variety of foods may be irradiated in Canada, including potatoes, onions, wheat, flour, whole wheat flour, whole and ground spices, and whole or ground dried seasoning vegetables. Some processed foods may also be irradiated, such as some ethnic foods, grain products and ready-to-eat meats. In order to be sold in Canada, all irradiated foods must be approved after a thorough safety assessment. This assessment takes into account the characteristics of the food, the purpose of the irradiation, the level of irradiation, and information related to packaging. The level of irradiation will not increase the radioactivity of the food. The type of food and the purpose of the irradiation determine the amount of radiation that is used. For example, potatoes may be irradiated to slow down the growth of roots and tubers, while spices may be irradiated to reduce microbial load. The safety assessment takes into account the potential changes that can occur to the food when it is irradiated, including the changes to the nutritional quality and the microbiological safety of the food. If the assessment identifies a safety concern, the food will not be approved for sale in Canada. The labelling requirements also help consumers make informed decisions about irradiated foods. Are irradiated foods available in Canada? Irradiated foods have been available in Canada for over 30 years and are available in a variety of products, including ground spices, dehydrated seasoning and potatoes. Currently, all domestic and imported foods that have been irradiated and sold in Canada are from the following categories: potatoes, onions, wheat, flour, whole wheat flour, whole and ground spices, and whole or ground dried seasoning vegetables. Some processed foods may also be irradiated. For example, some ethnic foods, grain products and ready-to-eat meats. Does Health Canada recommend the consumption of irradiated foods over foods that have not been irradiated? Health Canada supports informed consumer choice by requiring labelling of irradiated foods to alert consumers to their presence in the foods marketplace. The use of irradiation on foods is only one of several preservation techniques that help ensure the safety of the foods Canadians eat. Health Canada recommends that Canadians follow the general rules of food safety, which include proper food handling, preparation and storage. How is food irradiation regulated in Canada? Food irradiation is regulated in Canada under the Food and Drugs Act. Health Canada is responsible for assessing the safety of foods, including those that have been irradiated, through the pre-market safety assessment process for food additives and other novel foods. If the assessment identifies a safety concern, the food will not be approved for sale in Canada. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is responsible for compliance and enforcement of labelling regulations for irradiated foods. Does Health Canada have any research on the potential health effects of consuming irradiated foods? Health Canada has conducted a thorough safety assessment of the potential health effects of consuming irradiated foods. The assessment took into account the characteristics of the food, the purpose of the irradiation, the level of irradiation, and information related to packaging. The assessment found that irradiated foods are as safe and nutritious as their non-irradiated counterparts. The assessment also found that the irradiation process does not increase the radioactivity of the food. Health Canada continues to monitor the safety of irradiated foods through regular updates of the scientific literature and ongoing research. Are there any restrictions on the importation of irradiated foods into Canada? There are no specific restrictions on the importation of irradiated foods into Canada. However, all imported foods, including irradiated foods, must meet the requirements of the Food and Drugs Act and its associated regulations. The safety assessment is conducted by Health Canada and is based on the best available scientific evidence.
